traps: Solving x² − x − 1 = 0 by the formula and carrying √5 through the whole answer. You were only asked for α₁ + α₄. Use sum of roots = 1 and the √5 disappears before it ever appears.

Counting only the interior jumps and forgetting x = −1 and x = 2. At both ends the quadratic is exactly 5, and 5 is an isolated value of the function, so both ends are discontinuity points. Always check the end points of the given interval.

Adding both roots of a level equation without checking they lie in the given interval. Sum of roots is valid only when both roots are inside the domain. Here both roots of x² − x − 1 = 0 sit inside [−1, 2], so it is safe — confirm that first, every time.

title: Why greatest-integer questions are really about range
key_idea: This problem was hard, and not for the reason you think. The continuity part was one line; everything else was the greatest integer function.
one_line: A greatest-integer question is really a range question: find what the inside value ranges over, and each step of [x] reads off as 'integer included, next integer excluded'.
traps: Treating it as a hard continuity problem and burning time on limits. Continuity is one line here. Spend your time getting the greatest integer values right, portion by portion.
Putting a filled circle at the right end of a step. Left integer is included (filled), right integer is never reached (hollow). Only the next step owns it.
Forgetting the exact integer point, like x = 5. At x = 5 the greatest integer is 5, not 4. The exact integer always belongs to the new step.

title: Final answer 3, and why the graph was essential
key_idea: The final answer is a one-line sum: 3. The interesting part is that you could not have written down a single term of that sum without the picture.
one_line: The last step is pure addition — α₁+α₄+α₂+α₃+2−1 = 3 — but every α in it came from the graph, which alone showed that the quadratic runs from 2.75 up to 5 and so touches only 3, 4 and 5.
traps: Looking at the final sum and concluding the graph was decorative. The sum itself needs no graph — but α₁, α₂, α₃, α₄ were all read off the picture. Draw the graph first, collect the α's, then add.

Reading only the two end values, 5 and 5, and assuming the function stays between them. A parabola can sit far below both ends. Compute the minimum; here it is 2.75, which pins the values to the stretch 2.75 to 5 and limits the integers to 3, 4 and 5.
Expecting the exam to hand you a wide interval like this one. In the paper the interval will be short, which actually makes it easier. The method does not change: range, then the integers inside it.

title: Continuity of a Composite Function f(g(x)) at a Point
key_idea: If you start simplifying f(g(x)) piece by piece, you will lose ten minutes and probably the question. There is a three-value route that finishes it in forty seconds.
one_line: To test f(g(x)) at x = a, never build fog — find g(a⁺), g(a⁻) and g(a) as limits, feed those three into f, and compare the three answers.
traps: Simplifying f(g(x)) into one big piecewise function before checking anything. Never build fog for a continuity-at-a-point question. Work only with g(a⁺), g(a⁻), g(a) and feed them to f.
Writing g(2⁺) = 2 and g(2⁻) = 1 as flat numbers, then plugging into f. Keep them as limits — slightly bigger than 2, slightly smaller than 1 — so f takes the correct branch at its own breakpoint.
Writing the final limit as 7⁺ or 7⁻. The plus/minus is only for inputs. A final limit answer is always a clean number: the right hand limit of f at 2 is 7, full stop.

title: Quiz: Continuity of fog with a Signum Function
key_idea: This quiz looks dangerous. It is not. Nothing new is needed — the same three-value method, applied honestly, kills it in thirty seconds.
one_line: Even when g jumps at x = 1, fog can still be continuous there — check f(g(1⁻)), f(g(1)) and f(g(1⁺)), and if all three are +1, it is continuous.
traps: Choosing "cannot be determined" because the question looks frightening. That is answering from the heart, not from the maths. You can always determine it here. Compute the three values. If they come out equal, say continuous and move on — nobody gets marks for a feeling.

Assuming that because g is discontinuous at x = 1, f(g(x)) must also be discontinuous there. Wrong logic. A discontinuous inner function can still give a continuous composite. Only the three values of f(g(x)) decide it.

Forgetting that signum 0 = 0, and writing signum of a value as +1 just because it looks small and positive-ish. Check exactly: signum is +1 only for x > 0, −1 only for x < 0, and 0 at x = 0. If any one of the three inner values is exactly 0, that branch gives 0 and the composite usually breaks.

title: Wherever the Denominator is Zero the Function is Discontinuous
key_idea: Some discontinuities you have to hunt for with left-hand and right-hand limits. This one hands itself to you — just look at the bottom of the fraction.
one_line: Wherever the denominator of a function becomes zero (and the numerator does not), that point is outside the domain and the function is discontinuous there.
traps: Calling 1/x² continuous at x = 0 because the left-hand and right-hand limits are the same. They are both +∞, and infinity is not a value. For continuity the common limit must be finite and equal to f(0) — and f(0) does not even exist here.

Hunting for left-hand and right-hand limits at a point where the denominator is zero. No need. Zero denominator with a non-zero numerator means an infinite limit, which already settles it as discontinuous.

Writing down the roots of the denominator without glancing at the numerator. Put the value into the numerator too. The rule as taught needs a non-zero number on top — that is what forces the limit to blow up.

title: Points of Discontinuity of fog — the Inner-Function Trap
key_idea: This question looks like a two-line job: simplify fog, set the denominator to zero, done. That is exactly how the trap catches you, and it costs you the whole question.
one_line: For points of discontinuity of fog, the simplified denominator is only half the answer — you must also add every point where the inner g(x) itself blows up.
traps: Simplifying fog, reading only its denominator, and writing just x = 3. That is the one point the paper-setter wants you to tick. Also list every point where the inner g(x) is undefined — here x = 2 — because fog cannot exist where g does not.

Thinking that once (x-2) cancels from top and bottom, the point x = 2 is fine. Cancelling changes the expression, not the domain. The original fog was never defined at x = 2, so it stays discontinuous there.

Getting the denominator as x + 3 instead of 3 - x and answering x = -3. 1 - (x-2) means the minus distributes over both terms: 1 - x + 2 = 3 - x. This is an easy sign to drop — slow down for one second on that bracket.

title: Discontinuity of f(f(x)) with f(x) = 1/(1-x)
key_idea: For f(f(x)) with f(x) = 1/(1 − x), both x = 1, where the inner f dies, and x = 0, where the simplified form dies, are points of discontinuity.
one_line: For f(f(x)) with f(x) = 1/(1 − x), both x = 1 (where the inner f dies) and x = 0 (where the simplified form dies) are points of discontinuity.
traps: Answering only x = 0, because the final form (x − 1)/x shows only that denominator. Cancellation hides the inner failure. x = 1 was lost the moment you wrote f(x), so it is still a point of discontinuity of f(f(x)).

Substituting into f wrongly — replacing x by 1 − x instead of by the whole 1/(1 − x). f(f(x)) means the entire inner output goes into the slot. Write f(input) = 1/(1 − input) and then paste 1/(1 − x) as the input.
Simplifying first and only then thinking about the domain. Domain first, algebra second. Fix the forbidden points of the inner function before any cancellation happens.

title: Slope of the Chord AB and What Happens as h → 0
key_idea: One small line joining two points on a curve. Push those two points together and that same line becomes the tangent — and that one picture is where the derivative comes from.
one_line: The chord joining A(a, f(a)) and B(a+h, f(a+h)) has slope [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h, and as h → 0 that chord turns into the tangent at A.
traps: Writing f(a+h) as f(a) + h. f is a machine, not a number you can split. Put the whole a+h inside the function: for f(x) = 2x + 5, f(a+h) = 2(a+h) + 5.

Subtracting in opposite order on top and bottom, like [f(a+h) − f(a)] ÷ [a − (a+h)]. Keep B first and A second in both rows. Top: f(a+h) − f(a). Bottom: (a+h) − a = h. Mixing the order flips the sign of your slope.

Putting h = 0 straight into the slope of the chord. At h = 0 the points A and B are the same point and there is no chord at all. We say h tends to 0 — B comes as close as you like but stays a separate point.

title: Derivative at a Point Means Slope of the Tangent (First Principle)
one_line: The derivative at a point is nothing but the slope of the tangent there, and the limit f'(a) = lim(h→0) [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h is exactly that slope — the first principle.
traps: Putting h = 0 straight into [f(a+h) − f(a)]/h. You get 0/0, which means nothing. h only approaches 0 — first simplify the expression with a formula or identity, then take the limit.
Treating the derivative as a property of the whole curve instead of a point. The slope changes from point to point. f'(x) is the rule; f'(a) is the actual slope of the tangent at that one point a.

Believing the familiar one-sided picture is the full definition. In that picture B always came towards A from the right. The approach from the left side has to be checked too — that is the gap we close next.

title: Right Hand Derivative and Left Hand Derivative
one_line: Approaching the point from the right gives the right hand derivative f'(a+), and putting −h in place of h gives the left hand derivative f'(a−), with h positive in both.
traps: Taking h negative for the left hand derivative. h stays positive in both. You write a − h and divide by −h; h itself never turns negative.
In the left hand derivative, writing [f(a − h) − f(a)]/h. The denominator also has to become −h. You replaced h by −h everywhere, so the h downstairs changes too.

Thinking the left and right derivatives are two different answers for every function. For every common differentiable function — sin x, cos x, tan x, eˣ, xⁿ, aˣ — both give the identical answer. The two differ only in the special cases we take up next.

title: Differentiability Means a Unique Tangent
key_idea: A graph is differentiable at a point only if exactly one tangent can be drawn there: one tangent means differentiable, two means not.
one_line: A graph is differentiable at a point only if exactly one tangent can be drawn there — one tangent, differentiable; two tangents, not.
traps: Reading "unique tangent" as some heavy technical condition and freezing on the word. Unique just means one. If only one tangent can be drawn at that point, the graph is differentiable there. That is the whole sentence.

Thinking a kink is fine because the graph is still joined there, with no break. Joined is not enough. At a kink the two branches pull the tangent in two different directions, so the tangent is not unique and the graph is non-differentiable at that point.
Assuming a sharp corner is the only way differentiability can fail. It is one reason. A break in the graph — discontinuity at that point — is another, and we take that up next.

title: The Two Conditions for Differentiability at a Point
key_idea: In the last part a sharp corner killed differentiability. Now look at a graph that simply breaks at the point — and watch how easily you can draw two different tangents there.
one_line: A function is differentiable at x = a only if it is continuous at a and f'(a⁺) = f'(a⁻); if the graph breaks at a, it is 100% non-differentiable there.
traps: Checking only f'(a⁺) = f'(a⁻) and declaring the function differentiable, without first checking continuity at a. Continuity is condition one and it is compulsory. Verify continuity at x = a first; if it fails, write non-differentiable and stop.

Thinking a graph can be differentiable at a point where it breaks, because you managed to draw a tangent there. At a break you can draw two tangents — one on each branch. Differentiability needs a unique tangent, so a break means non-differentiable, with no exceptions.

Assuming a continuous graph is automatically differentiable. Continuity is only the first condition. The sharp corner graph was perfectly continuous and still non-differentiable because f'(a⁺) ≠ f'(a⁻).

title: Equal RHD and LHD Cannot Save a Discontinuous Graph
key_idea: If the graph breaks at x = a it is non-differentiable there, whatever the RHD and LHD turn out to be.
one_line: If the graph breaks at x = a, it is non-differentiable there — no matter what RHD and LHD turn out to be.
traps: Seeing RHD = LHD and immediately declaring the function differentiable. Equal slopes are only the second condition. If the function is not continuous at x = a, the answer is non-differentiable whatever the slopes are.
Believing that a discontinuous graph must have RHD ≠ LHD. It need not. You can easily draw a broken graph whose two tangents are parallel. The equality of slopes tells you nothing about the break.
Skipping the continuity check because the derivative work looks easier. Do continuity first. It is faster, and in these questions it finishes the problem by itself.

title: The Shortcut: Differentiate Each Piece and Put the Point In
key_idea: Check continuity first, then differentiate the x > a piece and put x = a into it for the RHD, and do the same with the x < a piece for the LHD.
one_line: For almost every question: check continuity first, then differentiate the x > a piece and put x = a in it for RHD, differentiate the x < a piece and put x = a in it for LHD.
traps: Jumping straight to the derivatives and skipping the continuity check. Write continuity first. A discontinuous point can never be differentiable, so that one line can finish the whole question.

Thinking that because both sides gave the same value, the function must be differentiable. That only proves continuity. Here both sides gave 3 and the function was still non-differentiable, because 0 ≠ 1.

Differentiating the wrong piece — using the x ≥ 0 definition to get the left hand derivative. RHD belongs to the piece valid for x > a only; LHD belongs to the piece valid for x < a only. Decide which definition applies before you differentiate.

title: Worked Example: A Piecewise Function That Is Differentiable at x = 1
key_idea: For f(x) = 2x² + x + 6 when x < 1 and x² + 3x + 5 when x ≥ 1, both sides give 9 at x = 1 and both derivatives give 5, so f is differentiable there.
one_line: For f(x) = 2x² + x + 6 when x < 1 and x² + 3x + 5 when x ≥ 1, both sides give 9 at x = 1 and both derivatives give 5, so f is differentiable at x = 1.
traps: Jumping straight to LHD and RHD without checking continuity. Continuity is the entry ticket. Match f(1⁻), f(1⁺) and f(1) first — here all three were 9 — and only then differentiate.

Taking the derivative of the wrong piece for the wrong side — using x² + 3x + 5 for the left hand derivative. x < 1 means left, so 2x² + x + 6 gives the LHD. x ≥ 1 means right, so x² + 3x + 5 gives the RHD. Decide the side before you differentiate.

Substituting x = 1 into the expression first and then trying to differentiate. Once you put the number in you only have a constant left. Differentiate while x is still there, and substitute at the very last step.

title: Same Derivatives but Discontinuous — Always Check Continuity First
key_idea: A discontinuity at a point settles the matter: the function is non-differentiable there, and equal LHD and RHD cannot rescue it.
one_line: A discontinuity at a point settles it — the function is non-differentiable there, and equal LHD and RHD cannot rescue it.
traps: Jumping straight into LHD and RHD without checking continuity. First compute the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and f(a). If they are not all equal, the answer is non-differentiable and the derivatives are not required.

Seeing LHD = RHD and writing "differentiable" in a hurry. Equal one-sided derivatives mean nothing across a jump. Continuity is the gate; only after it is passed does LHD = RHD decide differentiability.
Assuming the constant term is harmless because it differentiates to 0. It is harmless for the derivative, but it decides continuity. Here 1 + 3 + 7 = 11 against 9 is the entire answer.

title: The Three Cases Side by Side
key_idea: Differentiability at a point needs one unique tangent, so check continuity first and equal one-sided derivatives second — failing either one kills it.
one_line: Differentiability at a point needs one unique tangent, so check continuity first and equal one-sided derivatives second — failing either one kills it.
traps: Jumping straight to LHD and RHD without checking continuity, and then getting stuck. Check continuity at the point first. Only if it passes do you go on to the one-sided derivatives.
Thinking LHD = RHD is enough to call a point differentiable. Equal one-sided derivatives with a discontinuity still means two tangents, so it is non-differentiable. Both conditions must hold.

Assuming that if the graph breaks, the two derivatives must automatically come out unequal. They can easily be equal — the two pieces can have the same slope. A break is about the value, not the slope.

title: Oral Practice: Checking Differentiability at x = −1
key_idea: This one is an oral problem. No long working, no left-hand-limit drama — two numbers to match, two more numbers to match, and you are done.
one_line: At x = −1 the two pieces both give 0, and both derivatives give +2, so the function is continuous and differentiable there — value first, slope second.
traps: Jumping straight to the derivatives because the question only asks about differentiability. Continuity is part of the same question. Spend five seconds putting x = −1 in both pieces first. Skipping it costs you the marks even when your final answer happens to be right.

Assuming a nice-looking piecewise function must be continuous. Do not trust the look of it. Polynomials are continuous on their own, but the two pieces can still disagree at the joining point. Only the matched values prove it.

Differentiating −x² and writing the slope as 2x instead of −2x, so the sign at x = −1 comes out wrong. Carry the minus sign through the differentiation, then substitute. −2x at x = −1 gives +2, not −2.

title: Practice Set: Finding Constants for Continuity and Differentiability
key_idea: Two unknown constants at a joining point need two equations: one from continuity, one from LHD = RHD.
one_line: Two unknown constants at a joining point need two equations: one from continuity, one from LHD = RHD.
traps: Assuming the function is automatically continuous because the question says differentiable. Differentiable at a point forces continuity at that point. So write the continuity equation yourself — it is one of your two relations.
Equating the two pieces' values and calling that the derivative condition. Values matching is continuity. Slopes matching is differentiability. They are two separate equations and you need both.
Stopping after finding one constant. Solve the pair of equations together, then substitute both values back and check value and slope at the joining point.

title: Quiz Solutions: Shortest Route and the Time-Waster
key_idea: Matching the derivatives of the two pieces at the junction drops one constant out immediately; and once LHL ≠ RHL, stop — there is nothing left to differentiate.
one_line: Match the derivatives of the two pieces at the junction and one constant drops out instantly — and once LHL ≠ RHL, stop: there is nothing left to differentiate.
traps: Going into first principles to find the derivative of each piece when the pieces are simple polynomials. Just differentiate them normally and equate at the junction. Same marks, one line.
Computing LHD and RHD after you have already found LHL ≠ RHL. Stop at the limits. Discontinuous means non-differentiable — write that and move on.
Concluding "differentiable" because LHD came out equal to RHD, while the function was discontinuous there. Continuity is the entry ticket. If it fails, equal one-sided derivatives prove nothing.

title: Type 2: Defining the Function Piecewise Yourself (Modulus)
one_line: When the function is not handed to you piecewise — like f(x) = |x − 2026| — you open the modulus yourself, and then Type 2 becomes Type 1.
traps: Seeing that it is continuous and concluding it must be differentiable. Continuous does not mean differentiable. |x − 2026| is continuous at 2026 and still fails there. Always check the two derivatives separately.

Opening the mod for x < 2026 as x − 2026, forgetting the extra negative. Below 2026 the inside is a negative number, so the mod must flip its sign: −(x − 2026) = 2026 − x. Test with one number — at x = 2025, |2025 − 2026| = 1, and 2026 − 2025 = 1. It matches.

Trying to differentiate |x − 2026| in one shot, without splitting. A modulus has a corner. You cannot differentiate across it. Break it into two pieces first, then differentiate each piece on its own side.

title: The Three Types of Continuity–Differentiability Questions
key_idea: Every continuity–differentiability question in JEE is one of three types: the piecewise function is given, it has to be made piecewise, or the LHD/RHD definition must be used.
one_line: Every continuity–differentiability question in JEE is one of three types: the piecewise function is given, you have to make it piecewise yourself, or you must go back to the LHD/RHD definition.
traps: Writing out the LHD/RHD limit for every question because it feels safer. If each piece is a normal differentiable expression, just differentiate the pieces and match them at the breakpoint. Save the limit definition for the small Type 3 variety.

Starting to differentiate a modulus or greatest-integer function without splitting it. That is a Type 2 question. Split it piecewise first, note the breakpoints, then check continuity and differentiability at those points only.

title: Category 2 problems: define the function, then find LHD and RHD
key_idea: Six questions, ten minutes, and not one of them needs a new formula. They only check one thing: can you open the function before you differentiate it?
one_line: Category 2 is the define-the-function type: expand the mod, greatest integer or fractional part around the point first, and only then take RHD and LHD.
traps: Reading sin|x| as |sin x|, or |x² − 4| as x² − 4. The modulus sign is placed where it is on purpose. Read what is inside the bracket before you expand anything.
Writing "non-differentiable" and stopping there. A non-differentiable point still has a right hand derivative and a left hand derivative. Find both; they simply will not match.
Differentiating while the mod or the bracket is still sitting inside. First define the function in two pieces around the point, then differentiate each piece. Never the other way round.

title: RHD and LHD of e^|x|, |x|+sin|x| and |x|+cos|x| at x = 0
key_idea: Three functions, three mods, and all three break at the same point. Once you see how little work each one needs, you will stop fearing this type forever.
one_line: Split the mod into its two definitions, differentiate each branch, and compare f'(0+) with f'(0-) — for e^|x|, |x|+sin|x| and |x|+cos|x| they come out 1 and −1, 2 and −2, 1 and −1, so all three are continuous but non-differentiable at 0.
traps: Splitting cos|x| into two different formulas and wasting time. cos is even, so cos|x| = cos x for all x. Write that in one line and move on.
Differentiating e^(−x) as e^(−x) and losing the minus sign. Chain rule: d/dx e^(−x) = −e^(−x). That minus is exactly what makes f'(0−) = −1 instead of 1.

Assuming that because the graph has no break, the function must be differentiable. All three here are continuous at 0 and still non-differentiable. Continuity only needs the value to match; differentiability needs LHD = RHD.

title: (x−2)|x²−4|: differentiable at 2 but not at −2
key_idea: One function, two points where the mod dies, two opposite answers. Differentiable at x = 2, non-differentiable at x = −2 — and the only reason is a repeated factor.
one_line: For f(x) = (x−2)|x²−4|, the factor (x−2) is repeated at x = 2 so both one-sided derivatives are 0 and f is differentiable there, while at x = −2 the two branches give +16 and −16, so f is continuous but not differentiable.
traps: Opening |x² − 4| as x² − 4 everywhere and differentiating one single formula. Write the interval-wise definition first: positive for x ≤ −2 and x ≥ 2, negative for −2 < x < 2. Without that split both answers come out wrong.

Taking the wrong branch for the left and right side at x = −2. Slightly bigger than −2 means you are inside (−2, 2), so use the branch with the minus sign. Slightly smaller than −2 means you are in (−∞, −2), so use the plain branch. Read off the interval, do not guess.

Assuming a mod is automatically non-differentiable wherever the inside becomes 0. A zero of the inside is only a suspect point. Here x = 2 passes the test and x = −2 fails it, in the very same function. Always check LHD and RHD.

title: x²[x]: one-sided derivatives at x = −1, 0, 1 and 2
one_line: On each side of an integer replace [x] by its constant value, then differentiate: x²[x] breaks at every integer except x = 0, where the x² switches off the jump and it is both continuous and differentiable.
traps: Writing "discontinuous, non-differentiable" at x = 0 out of habit, because that is what greatest integer functions always do. This is the exact trap in this question. Do the process at 0 like anywhere else: right side gives 0, left side gives −x², both limits are 0 and both derivatives are 0. It is continuous and differentiable there.

Treating [x] as a varying thing and trying to differentiate it along with x². On one side of an integer, [x] does not move at all — it is a fixed number. Only x² varies, so differentiate just the x² and carry the constant along.

Jumping straight to LHD and RHD and never checking continuity. Check continuity first. If the two side limits differ, the point is already non-differentiable and you are done. Continuity never leaves the differentiability chapter.

title: Greatest integer with fractional part: 2[x]+3{x}−7x² at x = 0 and 1
one_line: On every interval replace [x] by its constant value and {x} by x − [x]; for f(x) = 2[x] + 3{x} − 7x² the two one-sided derivatives come out equal at x = 0 and x = 1, yet the function is non-differentiable there because continuity itself fails.
traps: Treating LHD = RHD as proof that the function is differentiable at that point. Equal one-sided derivatives mean nothing if the function is not continuous there. Here both sides give −11 at x = 1 and the answer is still non-differentiable. Always test continuity first.

Carrying [x] = 1 across to the left side of x = 1. On x slightly smaller than 1 you are in (0, 1), so [x] = 0 and {x} = x. The constant changes the moment you cross an integer, so write the interval down before substituting.

Freezing because [x] and {x} look like new, special functions. They are not. Convert them into a constant and a linear piece on each interval and the question becomes a polynomial question you have solved a hundred times.

title: Algebra of continuity and differentiability for f ± g, fg and f/g
key_idea: Two broken functions can add up to a perfectly smooth one. Once you see why, this whole topic becomes two numbers in your head instead of a theorem you memorise.
one_line: Continuous ± continuous stays continuous (and f/g too, as long as g ≠ 0), continuous ± discontinuous is always discontinuous, continuous × discontinuous is discontinuous only when the continuous limit is non-zero, and when both are discontinuous nothing can be said.
traps: Writing 'continuous × discontinuous = discontinuous' as a flat rule. Attach the condition. It is discontinuous provided the limit of the continuous function is not zero. Check that limit first — if it is 0, the product is continuous.

Assuming discontinuous + discontinuous must be discontinuous. It need not be. 5 + 7 = 12 and 8 + 4 = 12 gives a continuous sum from two discontinuous functions. In this case nothing can be said, so test with numbers every time.

Quoting f/g as continuous or differentiable with no condition. Always add g ≠ 0. Where g = 0 the quotient is discontinuous, and since differentiating a quotient puts g² in the denominator, it is non-differentiable there too.

title: Old IIT MCQ: which function is differentiable at x = 0, decided by inspection
key_idea: Four options, one question: which one is differentiable at x = 0? You can kill two of them in five seconds flat, without defining a single function piecewise.
one_line: cos|x| is just cos x, so in this old IIT MCQ only the sin|x| options need real work — and the difference sin|x| − |x| is the one that is differentiable at x = 0.
traps: Seeing a mod sign inside cos and declaring cos|x| non-differentiable at 0. cos is even, so cos|x| = cos x exactly. There is no corner. Only an odd function like sin keeps the damage: sin|x| really does have a kink at 0.

Assuming non-differentiable + non-differentiable must be non-differentiable, so both (C) and (D) are rejected. There is no such rule. Two corners can cancel. Compute the left and right derivatives: (C) gives −2 and +2, (D) gives 0 and 0.

Writing out a full piecewise definition or reaching for the printed solution. Reaching for the printed solution costs you the time this question was meant to save. Just differentiate the x > 0 form and the x < 0 form directly and compare the two numbers at 0.

title: Category 3: derivative-looking limits solved by L'Hôpital, not by definition
key_idea: When a limit looks like a derivative but is plain 0/0, check the form instead of reaching for first principles: differentiate with respect to h, and remember f(a) is a constant whose derivative is 0, not f'(a).
one_line: When a limit looks like a derivative but is plain 0/0, don't reach for the first-principles definition — check the form, differentiate with respect to h, and remember f(a) is a constant whose derivative is 0, not f'(a).
traps: Differentiating f(a) as f'(a). f(a) is just a number — 10, 50, 200, whatever f gives at a. The derivative of a number with respect to h is 0. Write 0.

Writing f'(a+2h²) and forgetting the chain-rule factor 4h, or forgetting the minus sign inside f(2−h²). Always multiply by the derivative of the inside bracket. 2h² gives +4h; 2−h² gives −2h, and that minus turns the −5 into +10h f'(2−h²).

Forcing the first-principles definition on these because the shape looks like a derivative. Keep the definition for genuine helplessness. If it is 0/0 and you can differentiate, differentiate. Here there was no helplessness at all.

title: Quiz: [f(5+t)−f(5−t)]/2t and the chain-rule sign trap
key_idea: The derivative of f(5−t) with respect to t is −f'(5−t), so [f(5+t) − f(5−t)]/2t tends to f'(5) rather than 0; and [f(x) − f(2)]/(x − 2) is simply f'(2).
one_line: The derivative of f(5−t) with respect to t is −f'(5−t), so limit [f(5+t)−f(5−t)]/2t comes out as 2f'(5)/2 = f'(5), not 0 — and limit [f(x)−f(2)]/(x−2) is simply f'(2).
traps: Differentiating f(5−t) as f'(5−t) and getting f'(5) − f'(5) = 0. The inside 5−t has derivative −1, so you get +f'(5−t). The two terms add: 2f'(5)/2 = f'(5).
Differentiating f(2) as f'(2) while differentiating with respect to x. f(2) is a constant. Its derivative is 0, so the answer of [f(x) − f(2)]/(x − 2) as x → 2 is f'(2) from the f(x) term alone.

Differentiating top and bottom straight away, without checking the form. Substitute the value first. Only when it is 0/0 are you allowed to differentiate — that is why f(5) − f(5) = 0 is written out before anything else is touched.

title: Why the first-principles definition has not been needed so far
key_idea: You have differentiated hundreds of functions this year without once writing a limit. Did you ever ask why the definition never showed up?
one_line: Every formula you have been using — sin x, cos x, x² — was itself built from the LHD/RHD definition, which is why direct differentiation has been enough so far.
traps: Treating the formula list and the definition as two unrelated things, so the definition feels useless. They are the same thing. The formulas came out of the definition — so using a formula is using the definition in compressed form.
Not knowing the LHD and RHD statement by heart, because "we never use it". Write both from memory today. The questions that actually carry weight are the ones where only the definition works.
Mixing up the denominator sign in LHD — writing f(a−h) − f(a) over h. If you step to a − h, the step size is −h. Keep the denominator −h in LHD and h in RHD.

title: x² sin(1/x) at x = 0: when you must go back to the definition
one_line: For f(x) = x² sin(1/x) with f(0) = 0, the direct derivative collapses into cos(1/x) at 0, so you go back to the first-principles definition and get RHD = LHD = 0 — continuous and differentiable.
traps: Calling the function non-differentiable because 2x sin(1/x) − cos(1/x) has no value at x = 0. That formula is only valid for x ≠ 0. The failure of the formula proves nothing — check with the definition, and here the answer comes out to a clean 0.

Giving sin(1/x) or cos(1/x) some value at x → 0, or treating it as a limit that exists. Write it as an oscillating number with no fixed value, but always finite between −1 and +1. That is all you need, and it is all you can honestly say.

Forgetting to subtract f(0) in the definition, or using x² sin(1/x) instead of the given f(0) = 0. f(0) comes from the second line of the definition of the function: f(0) = 0. Put f(h) = h² sin(1/h) and f(0) = 0, then the quotient reduces to h sin(1/h).

Doing the whole left hand derivative again from scratch. Put −h in place of h: one negative appears on top and one in the denominator, they cancel, and you already had 0. So LHD = RHD = 0 with no extra work.

title: Contrast: x sin(1/x) is continuous but non-differentiable at 0
key_idea: x sin(1/x) with f(0) = 0 is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there: the difference quotient collapses to sin(1/h), which merely oscillates between −1 and 1.
one_line: x sin(1/x) with f(0) = 0 is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there, because the difference quotient collapses to sin(1/h), which just oscillates between −1 and 1.
traps: Assuming that because it is continuous at 0, it must be differentiable at 0. Continuity is a weaker condition. x sin(1/x) is the clean counter-example — continuous at 0, derivative at 0 missing. Always test the derivative separately from the definition.

Writing lim(h→0) sin(1/h) = 0 because 'sin of something small is small'. 1/h is not small when h → 0, it is huge. sin(1/h) oscillates in [−1, 1] and has no limit. Only a factor of h in front can save it, by the squeeze.

Differentiating x sin(1/x) by product rule and putting x = 0 in the answer. That formula is valid only for x ≠ 0. At the single point x = 0 the function is defined piecewise, so f′(0) must come from the first-principle limit.
